Scaling Laws in Linear Regression:
Compute, Parameters, and Data

Licong Lin ††thanks: UC Berkeley. Email: liconglin@berkeley.edu    Jingfeng Wu ††thanks: UC Berkeley. Email: uuujf@berkeley.edu    Sham M. Kakade ††thanks: Harvard University. Email: sham@seas.harvard.edu    Peter L. Bartlett ††thanks: UC Berkeley and Google DeepMind. Email: peter@berkeley.edu    Jason D. Lee ††thanks: Princeton University. Email: jasonlee@princeton.edu
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Empirically, large-scale deep learning models often satisfy a neural scaling law: the test error of the trained model improves polynomially as the model size and data size grow. However, conventional wisdom suggests the test error consists of approximation, bias, and variance errors, where the variance error increases with model size. This disagrees with the general form of neural scaling laws, which predict that increasing model size monotonically improves performance.

We study the theory of scaling laws in an infinite dimensional linear regression setup. Specifically, we consider a model with MM parameters as a linear function of sketched covariates. The model is trained by one-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD) using NN data. Assuming the optimal parameter satisfies a Gaussian prior and the data covariance matrix has a power-law spectrum of degree a>1a>1, we show that the reducible part of the test error is Θ(M−(a−1)+N−(a−1)/a)\Theta(M^{-(a-1)}+N^{-(a-1)/a}). The variance error, which increases with MM, is dominated by the other errors due to the implicit regularization of SGD, thus disappearing from the bound. Our theory is consistent with the empirical neural scaling laws and verified by numerical simulation.

1 Introduction

Deep learning models, particularly those on a large scale, are pivotal in advancing the state-of-the-art across various fields. Recent empirical studies have shed light on the so-called neural scaling laws (see Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022, for example), which suggest that the generalization performance of these models improves polynomially as both model size, denoted by MM, and data size, denoted by NN, increase. The neural scaling law quantitatively describes the population risk as:

ℛ⁡(M,N)≈ℛ∗+c1Ma1+c2Na2,\mathcal{R}(M,N)\approx\mathcal{R}^{*}+\frac{c_{1}}{M^{a_{1}}}+\frac{c_{2}}{N^{a_{2}}}, (1)

where ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*} is a positive irreducible risk and c1c_{1}, c2c_{2}, a1a_{1}, a2a_{2} are positive constants independent of MM and NN. For instance, by fitting the above formula with empirical measurements in standard large-scale language benchmarks, Hoffmann et al. (2022) estimated a1≈0.34a_{1}\approx 0.34 and a2≈0.28a_{2}\approx 0.28, while Besiroglu et al. (2024) estimated that a1≈0.35a_{1}\approx 0.35 and a2≈0.37a_{2}\approx 0.37. Though the exact exponents depend on the tasks, neural scaling laws in Equation 1 are observed consistently in practice and are used as principled guidance to build state-of-the-art models, especially under a compute budget (Hoffmann et al., 2022).

From the perspective of statistical learning theory, Equation 1 is rather intriguing. Standard statistical learning bounds (see Mohri et al., 2018; Wainwright, 2019, for example) often decompose the population risk into the sum of irreducible error, approximation error, bias error, and variance error (some theory replaces bias and variance errors by optimization and generalization errors, respectively) as in the form of

ℛ⁡(M,N)=ℛ∗+𝒪⁡(1Ma1)⏟approximation+𝒪⁡(1Na2)⏟bias+𝒪⁡(c⁡(M)Na3)⏟variance,\mathcal{R}(M,N)={\mathcal{R}^{*}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}\bigg(\frac{1}{M^{a_{1}}}\bigg)}_{\text{approximation}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{a_{2}}}\bigg)}_{\text{bias}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}\bigg(\frac{c(M)}{N^{a_{3}}}\bigg)}_{\text{variance}}, (2)

where a1,a2,a3a_{1},a_{2},a_{3} are positive constants and c⁡(M)c(M) is a measure of model complexity that typically increases with the model size MM. In Equation 2, the approximation error is induced by the mismatch of the best-in-class predictor and the best possible predictor, hence decreasing with the model size MM. The bias error is induced by the mismatch of the expected algorithm output and the best-in-class predictor, hence decreasing with the data size NN. The variance error measures the uncertainty of the algorithm output, which decreases with the data size NN but increases with the model size MM (since the model complexity c⁡(M)c(M) increases).

A mystery.

The empirical neural scaling law Equation 1 is incompatible with the typical statistical learning theory bound Equation 2. While the two error terms in the neural scaling law Equation 1 can be explained by the approximation and bias errors in the theoretical bound Equation 2 respectively, it is not clear why the variance error is unobservable when fitting the neural scaling law empirically. This difference must be reconciled, otherwise, the statistical learning theory and the empirical scaling law make conflict predictions: as the model size MM increases, the theoretical bound Equation 2 predicts an increase of variance error that eventually causes an increase of the population risk, but the neural scaling law Equation 1 predicts a decrease of the population risk. In other words, it remains unclear when to follow the prediction of the empirical scaling law Equation 1 and when to follow that of the statistical learning bound Equation 2.

Certain prior works provided risk upper bounds that do not grow with model size (see for example (Rudi and Rosasco, 2017; Carratino et al., 2018)). Still, their results are insufficient for studying scaling law as those bounds require a large model size such that the approximation error is ignorable. Moreover, they do not provide instance-wise matching lower bounds to verify the tightness of the upper bounds. See a detailed discussion in Section 2.

Our explanation.

We investigate this issue in an infinite dimensional linear regression setup. We only assume access to MM-dimensional sketched covariates given by a fixed Gaussian sketch and their responses. We consider a linear predictor with MM trainable parameters, which is trained by one-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with geometrically decaying stepsizes using NN sketched data. Assuming that the spectrum of the data covariance matrix satisfies a power-law of degree a>1a>1 and that the optimal model parameters satisfy a Gaussian prior, we derive matching upper and lower bounds on the population risk achieved by the SGD output (see Theorem 4.1). Specifically, we show that

ℛ⁡(M,N)=ℛ∗+Θ​(1Ma−1)+Θ~​(1(N​γ)(a−1)/a)⏟leading order given by the sum of 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 and 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌,𝖵𝖺𝗋=Θ~​(min⁡{M,(N​γ)1/a}N)⏟higher order, thus unobservable,\mathcal{R}(M,N)=\mathcal{R}^{*}+\underbrace{\Theta\bigg(\frac{1}{M^{a-1}}\bigg)+\tilde{\Theta}\bigg(\frac{1}{(N\gamma)^{(a-1)/a}}\bigg)}_{\text{leading order given by the sum of $\mathsf{Approx}$ and $\mathsf{Bias}$}},\quad\mathsf{Var}=\underbrace{\tilde{\Theta}\bigg(\frac{\min\{M,(N\gamma)^{1/a}\}}{N}\bigg)}_{\text{higher order, thus unobservable}},

where γ=𝒪⁡(1)\gamma=\mathcal{O}(1) is the initial stepsize used in SGD and Θ~​(⋅)\tilde{\Theta}(\cdot) hides log⁡(N)\log(N) factors. In our bound, the sum of the approximation and bias errors determines the order of the excess risk, while the variance error is of a strictly higher order and is therefore nearly unobservable when fitting ℛ⁡(M,N)\mathcal{R}(M,N) as a function of MM and NN empirically. In addition, our analysis reveals that the small variance error is due to the implicit regularization effect of one-pass SGD (Zou et al., 2021). Our theory suggests that the empirical neural scaling law Equation 1 is a simplification of the statistical learning bound Equation 2 in a special regime when strong regularization (either implicit or explicit) is employed.

Moreover, we generalize the above scaling law to (1) constant stepsize SGD with iterate average (see Theorem F.6), (2) cases where the optimal model parameter satisfies an anisotropic prior (see Theorem 4.2), and (3) where the spectrum of the data covariance matrix satisfies a logarithmic power law (see Theorem 4.3).

Emprical evidence.

Based on our theoretical results, we conjecture that the clean neural scaling law Equation 1 observed in practice is due to the disappearance of variance error caused by strong regularization. Two pieces of empirical evidence to support our understanding. First, large language models that follow the scaling law Equation 1 are often underfitted, as the models are trained over a single pass or a few passes over the data (Komatsuzaki, 2019; Muennighoff et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023). When models are underfitted, the variance error tends to be smaller. Second, when language models are trained with multiple passes (up to 77 passes), Muennighoff et al. (2023) found that the clean scaling law in Equation 1 no longer holds and they proposed a more sophisticated scaling law to explain their data. This can be explained by a relatively large variance error caused by multiple passes.

2 Related work

Empirical scaling laws.

In recent years, the scaling laws of deep neural networks in compute, sample size, and model size have been widely studied across different models and domains (Hestness et al., 2017; Rosenfeld et al., 2019; Kaplan et al., 2020; Henighan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Zhai et al., 2022; Muennighoff et al., 2023). The early work by Kaplan et al. (2020) first proposed the neural scaling laws of transformer-based models. They observed that the test loss exhibits a power-law decay in quantities including the amount of compute, sample size, and model size, and provided joint formulas in these quantities to predict the test loss. The proposed formulas were later generalized and refined in subsequent works (Henighan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Alabdulmohsin et al., 2022; Caballero et al., 2022; Muennighoff et al., 2023). Notably, Hoffmann et al. (2022) proposed the Chinchilla law, that is, Equation 1 with a1≈0.34a_{1}\approx 0.34 and a2≈0.28a_{2}\approx 0.28. The empirical observation guided them to allocate data and model size under a given compute budget. The Chinchilla law is further revised by Besiroglu et al. (2024). Motivated by the Chinchilla law, Muennighoff et al. (2023) considered the effect of multiple passes over training data and empirically fitted a more sophisticated scaling law that takes account of the effect of data reusing.

Theory of scaling laws.

Although neural scaling laws have been empirically observed over a broad spectrum of problems, there is a relatively limited literature on understanding these scaling laws from a theoretical perspective (Sharma and Kaplan, 2020; Bahri et al., 2021; Maloney et al., 2022; Hutter, 2021; Wei et al., 2022; Michaud et al., 2024; Jain et al., 2024; Bordelon et al., 2024; Atanasov et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2024; Dohmatob et al., 2024). Among these works, Sharma and Kaplan (2020) showed that the test loss scales as N4/dN^{4/d} for regression on data with intrinsic dimension dd. Hutter (2021) studied a toy problem under which a non-trivial power of NN arises in the test loss. Jain et al. (2024) considered scaling laws in data selection. Bahri et al. (2021) considered a linear teacher-student model under a power-law spectrum assumption on the covariates, and they showed that the test loss of the ordinary least square estimator decreases following a power law in sample size NN (resp. model size MM) when the model size MM (resp. sample size NN) is infinite. Bordelon et al. (2024) considered a linear random feature model and analyzed the test loss of the solution found by (batch) gradient flow. They focused on the bottleneck regimes where two of the quantities N,MN,M, TT (training steps) are infinite and showed that the risk has a power-law decay in the remaining quantity. The problem in Bahri et al. (2021); Bordelon et al. (2024) can be viewed as a sketched linear regression model similar to ours. It should be noted that both Bahri et al. (2021) and Bordelon et al. (2024) only derived the dependence of population risk on one of the data size, model size, or training steps in the asymptotic regime where the remaining quantities go to infinity, and their derivations are based on statistical physics heuristics. In comparison, we prove matching (ignoring constant factors) upper and lower risk bounds jointly depending on the finite model size MM and data size NN.

Implicit regularization of SGD.

One-pass SGD in linear regression has been extensively studied in both the classical finite-dimensional setting (Polyak and Juditsky, 1992; Bach and Moulines, 2013; Défossez and Bach, 2015; Dieuleveut et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2017; Ge et al., 2019) and the modern high-dimensional setting (Dieuleveut and Bach, 2015; Berthier et al., 2020; Zou et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022a; Wu et al., 2022b; Varre et al., 2021). In particular, Zou et al. (2021) showed that SGD induces an implicit regularization effect that is comparable to, and in certain cases even more preferable than, the explicit regularization effect induced by ridge regression. This is one of the key motivations of our scaling law interpretation. From a technical perspective, we utilize the sharp finite-sample and dimension-free analysis of SGD developed by Zou et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2022a); Wu et al. (2022b). Different from them, we consider a sequence of linear regression models with an increasing number of trainable parameters given by data sketch. Our main technical innovation is to sharply control the effect of data sketch. Some of our intermediate results, for example, tight bounds on the spectrum of the sketched data covariance under the power law (see Lemma 6.2), might be of independent interest.

Prior works investigated linear regression with random features (Rudi and Rosasco, 2017; Carratino et al., 2018), which can be viewed as a kind of sketched features via random coordinate selection. They mainly focused on the small approximation error regime, where the model size (or the number of features) is much larger than the data size. In comparison, we treat both model size and data size as free variables. Moreover, we provide matching upper and lower bounds while prior works mainly focused on upper bounds. These two innovations are crucial for studying scaling laws that predict test error as a function of both model size and data size. Finally, in the comparable regimes with small or zero approximation error, our excess risk bounds recover the bounds in prior works (Rudi and Rosasco, 2017; Carratino et al., 2018; Pillaud-Vivien et al., 2018; Dieuleveut and Bach, 2015; Defilippis et al., 2024).

3 Setup

We denote a feature vector by 𝐱∈ℍ\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{H}, where ℍ\mathbb{H} is a Hilbert space that is either finite-dimensional or countably infinite-dimensional, with dimension d:=dim(ℍ)d:=\dim(\mathbb{H}). The corresponding label is denoted by y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}. In linear regression, we measure the population risk of a parameter 𝐰∈ℍ\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{H} by the mean squared error,

ℛ⁡(𝐰)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}) :=𝔼​(⟨𝐱,𝐰⟩−y)2,𝐰∈ℍ,\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}\big(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}\rangle-y\big)^{2},\quad\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{H},

where the expectation is over (𝐱,y)∼P(\mathbf{x},y)\sim{P} for some distribution P{P} on ℍ×ℝ\mathbb{H}\times{\mathbb{R}}.

Let 𝐰∗∈arg⁡min𝐰⁡ℛ⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{w}^{*}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}) be the optimal model parameter11 1 If arg⁡min​ℛ​(⋅)\arg\min\mathcal{R}(\cdot) is not unique, we choose 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} to be the minimizer with minimal 𝐇\mathbf{H}-norm.. Assume that ‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2:=(𝐰∗)⊤​𝐇𝐰∗\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}:=(\mathbf{w}^{*})^{\top}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}^{*} is finite.

We only assume access to MM-dimensional sketched covariates and their responses, that is, (𝐒𝐱,y)(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},y), where 𝐒∈ℝM×ℍ\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}\times\mathbb{H} is a fixed sketch matrix. We focus on the Gaussian sketch matrix22 2 Our results can be extended to other sketching methods (see Woodruff et al., 2014, for example)., that is, entries of 𝐒\mathbf{S} are independently sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,1/M).\mathcal{N}\big(0,1/M\big). We then consider linear predictors with MM trainable parameters given by

f𝐯:ℍ→ℝ,𝐱↦⟨𝐯,𝐒𝐱⟩,f_{\mathbf{v}}:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{R},\quad\mathbf{x}\mapsto\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}\rangle,

where 𝐯∈ℝM\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} are the trainable parameters. Varying MM should be viewed as a linear analog of varying the neural network model size. Our sketched linear regression setting is comparable to the teacher-student setting considered by Bahri et al. (2021); Bordelon et al. (2024).

We consider the training of f𝐯f_{\mathbf{v}} via one-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD), that is,

𝐯t\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{t} :=𝐯t−1−γt​(f𝐯t−1​(𝐱t)−yt)​∇𝐯f𝐯t−1​(𝐱t)\displaystyle:=\mathbf{v}_{t-1}-\gamma_{t}\big(f_{\mathbf{v}_{t-1}}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-y_{t}\big)\nabla_{\mathbf{v}}f_{\mathbf{v}_{t-1}}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) (SGD)
:=𝐯t−1−γt​(𝐱t⊤​𝐒⊤​𝐯t−1−yt)​𝐒𝐱t,\displaystyle:=\mathbf{v}_{t-1}-\gamma_{t}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}_{t-1}-y_{t}\big)\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}_{t}, t=1,…,N,\displaystyle t=1,\dots,N,

for t=1,…,N,γt:=γ/2ℓ,where​ℓ=⌊t/(N/log⁡(N))⌋.\text{for $t=1,\dots,N$},\ \gamma_{t}:=\gamma/2^{\ell},\ \text{where}\ \ell=\lfloor t/(N/\log(N))\rfloor. (3)

Here, the initial stepsize γ\gamma is a hyperparameter for the SGD algorithm. Without loss of generality, we assume the initial parameter is 𝐯0=0\mathbf{v}_{0}=0. The output of the SGD algorithm is the last iterate 𝐯N\mathbf{v}_{N}. Our proof techniques apply to other stepsize schedulers (e.g., polynomial decay) as well, but we focus on geometric decay as it is known to achieve near minimax-optimal excess risk for the last iterate of SGD (Ge et al., 2019).

Conditioning on a sketch matrix 𝐒∈ℝM×ℍ\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}\times\mathbb{H}, each parameter 𝐯∈ℝM\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} induces a sketched predictor through 𝐱↦⟨𝐒⊤​𝐯,𝐱⟩\mathbf{x}\mapsto\langle\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v},\mathbf{x}\rangle, and we denote its risk by

ℛM​(𝐯):=ℛ⁡(𝐒⊤​𝐯)=𝔼​(⟨𝐒𝐱,𝐯⟩−y)2,𝐯∈ℝM.\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}):=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v})=\mathbb{E}\big(\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}\rangle-y\big)^{2},\quad\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}.

By increasing MM and NN, we have a sequence of datasets and trainable parameters of increasing sizes, respectively. This prepares us to study the scaling law Equation 1 in the sketched linear regression problem, that is, to understand ℛM​(𝐯N)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N}) as a function of both MM and NN.

Risk decomposition.

In a standard way, we decompose the risk achieved by 𝐯N\mathbf{v}_{N}, the last iterate of (SGD), to the sum of irreducible risk, approximization error, and excess risk as follows,

ℛM​(𝐯N)=min⁡ℛ⁡(⋅)⏟𝖨𝗋𝗋𝖾𝖽𝗎𝖼𝗂𝖻𝗅𝖾+min⁡ℛM​(⋅)−min⁡ℛ⁡(⋅)⏟𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑+ℛM​(𝐯N)−min⁡ℛM​(⋅)⏟𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌.\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})=\underbrace{\min\mathcal{R}(\cdot)}_{\mathsf{Irreducible}}+\underbrace{\min\mathcal{R}_{M}(\cdot)-\min\mathcal{R}(\cdot)}_{\mathsf{Approx}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})-\min\mathcal{R}_{M}(\cdot)}_{\mathsf{Excess}}. (4)

We emphasize that the irreducible risk is independent of MM and NN and thus can be viewed as a constant; the approximation error is determined by the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, thus depends on MM but is independent of NN; the excess risk depends on both MM and NN as it is determined by the algorithm.

4 Scaling laws

We first demonstrate a scaling-law behavior when the data spectrum satisfies a power law.

Assumption 1 (Distributional conditions).

Assume the following about the data distribution.

  1. A.

    Gaussian design.  Assume that 𝐱∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐇)\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{H}).

  2. B.

    Well-specified model.  Assume that 𝔼⁡[y|𝐱]=𝐱⊤​𝐰∗\mathbb{E}[y|\mathbf{x}]=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{w}^{*}. Define σ2:=𝔼​(y−𝐱⊤​𝐰∗)2\sigma^{2}:=\mathbb{E}(y-\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{w}^{*})^{2}.

  3. C.

    Parameter prior.  Assume that 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} satisfies a prior such that 𝔼​(𝐰∗)⊗2=𝐈\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{w}^{*})^{\otimes 2}=\mathbf{I}.

Assumption 2 (Power-law spectrum).

There exists a>1a>1 such that the eigenvalues of 𝐇\mathbf{H} satisfy λi≂i−a\lambda_{i}\eqsim i^{-a}, i>0i>0.

Theorem 4.1 (Scaling law).

Suppose that 1 and 2 hold. Consider an MM-dimensional sketched predictor trained by Equation SGD with NN samples. Let N𝚎𝚏𝚏:=N/log⁡(N)N_{\mathtt{eff}}:=N/\log(N) and recall the risk decomposition in Equation 4. Then there exists some aa-dependent constant c>0c>0 such that when the initial stepsize γ≤c\gamma\leq c, with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, we have

  1. 1.

    𝖨𝗋𝗋𝖾𝖽𝗎𝖼𝗂𝖻𝗅𝖾:=ℛ⁡(𝐰∗)=σ2\mathsf{Irreducible}:=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}^{*})=\sigma^{2}.

  2. 2.

    𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≂M1−a.{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx}\eqsim M^{1-a}.

  3. 3.

    Suppose in addition σ2≳1\sigma^{2}\gtrsim 1. The expected excess risk (𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Excess}) can be decomposed into a bias error (𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌\mathsf{Bias}) and a variance error (𝖵𝖺𝗋\mathsf{Var}), namely,

    𝔼​𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌≂𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌+σ2​𝖵𝖺𝗋,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathsf{Excess}\eqsim\mathsf{Bias}+\sigma^{2}\mathsf{Var},

    where the expectation is over the randomness of 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} and (𝐱i,yi)i=1N(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{N}. Moreover, 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌\mathsf{Bias} and 𝖵𝖺𝗋\mathsf{Var} satisfy

    𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌\displaystyle\mathsf{Bias} ≲max⁡{M1−a,(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a−1},\displaystyle\lesssim\max\big\{M^{1-a},\ (N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a-1}\big\},
    𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌\displaystyle\mathsf{Bias} ≳(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a−1​ when ​(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a≤M/c​ for some constant ​c>0,\displaystyle\gtrsim(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a-1}\text{ when }(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a}\leq M/c\text{\hskip 10.22217ptfor some constant }c>0,
    𝖵𝖺𝗋\displaystyle\mathsf{Var} ≂min⁡{M,(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a}/N𝚎𝚏𝚏.\displaystyle\eqsim{\min\big\{M,\ (N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a}\big\}}/{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}.

In all results, the hidden constants only depend on the power-law degree aa. As a direct consequence, when σ2≂1\sigma^{2}\eqsim 1, it holds with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S} that

𝔼​ℛM​(𝐯N)=σ2+Θ⁡(1Ma−1)+Θ⁡(1(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)(a−1)/a),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})=\sigma^{2}+\Theta\bigg(\frac{1}{M^{a-1}}\bigg)+\Theta\bigg(\frac{1}{(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{(a-1)/a}}\bigg),

where the expectation is over the randomness of 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} and (𝐱i,yi)i=1N(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{N}.

Theorem 4.1 shows a sharp (up to constant factors) scaling law risk bound under an isotroptic prior assumption and the power-law spectrum assumption. We emphasize that the scaling law bound in Theorem 4.1 holds for every M,N≥1M,N\geq 1. We also remark that the sum of approximization and bias errors dominates 𝔼​ℛM​(𝐯N)−σ2\mathbb{E}\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})-\sigma^{2}, whereas the variance error is of strict higher order in terms of both MM and NN, and is thus disappeared in the population risk bound.

Optimal stepsize.

Based on the tight scaling law in Theorem 4.1, we can calculate the optimal stepsize that minimizes the risk. Specifically, the optimal stepsize is γ≂1\gamma\eqsim 1 when N𝚎𝚏𝚏≲MaN_{\mathtt{eff}}\lesssim M^{a} and can be anything such that Ma/N𝚎𝚏𝚏≲γ≲1{M^{a}}/{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}\lesssim\gamma\lesssim 1 when N𝚎𝚏𝚏≳MaN_{\mathtt{eff}}\gtrsim M^{a}. In both cases, choosing γ≂1\gamma\eqsim 1 is optimal. When the sample size is large such that N𝚎𝚏𝚏≳MaN_{\mathtt{eff}}\gtrsim M^{a}, the optimal stepsize is relatively robust and can be chosen from a range.

Allocation of data and model sizes.

Following Hoffmann et al. (2022), we measure the compute complexity by M​NMN as Equation SGD queries MM-dimensional gradients for NN times. Given a total compute budget of M​N=CMN=C, from Theorem 6.1 and N𝚎𝚏𝚏:=N/log⁡(N)N_{\mathtt{eff}}:=N/\log(N), we see that the best population risk is achieved by setting γ=Θ⁡(1)\gamma=\Theta(1), M=Θ~​(C1/(a+1))M=\tilde{\Theta}(C^{1/(a+1)}), and N=Θ~​(Ca/(a+1))N=\tilde{\Theta}(C^{a/(a+1)}). Our theory suggests setting a data size slightly larger than the model size when the compute budget is the bottleneck.

Comparison with (Bordelon et al., 2024).

The work by Bordelon et al. (2024) considered the scaling law of batch gradient descent (or gradient flow) on a teacher-student model (see their equation (14)). Their teacher-student model can be viewed as our sketched linear regression model. However, we consider one-pass SGD, therefore in our setting the number of gradient steps is equivalent to the data size. When we equalize the number of gradient steps and the data size in their equation (14) and set the parameter prior as 1C, their prediction is consistent with ours. However, our analysis shows the computational advantage of SGD over batch GD since each iteration requires only 1/N1/N the compute. Bordelon et al. (2024) obtained the limit of the population risk as two out of the data size, model size, and the number of gradient steps go to infinity based on statistical physics heuristics. In comparison, we obtain upper and lower risk bounds that hold for any finite MM and NN and match ignoring a constant factor depending only on the spectrum power-law degree aa.

Average of the SGD iterates

Results similar to Theorem 4.1 can also be established for the average of the iterates of online SGD with constant stepsize (Polyak and Juditsky, 1992; Dieuleveut et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2023). All results will be the same once replacing the effective sample size N𝚎𝚏𝚏N_{\mathtt{eff}} in Theorem 4.1 to the sample size NN. For more details see Theorem F.6 in Appendix F.

4.1 Scaling law under source condition

The isotropic parameter prior condition (1C) in Theorem 4.1 can be generalized to the following anisotropic version (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007).

Assumption 3 (Source condition).

Let (λi,𝐯i)i>0(\lambda_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i})_{i>0} be the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 𝐇\mathbf{H}. Assume 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} satisfies a prior such that

for i≠j,𝔼⁡⟨𝐯i,𝐰∗⟩​⟨𝐯j,𝐰∗⟩=0;and for i>0,𝔼​λi​⟨𝐯i,𝐰∗⟩2≂i−b, for some b>1.\text{for $i\neq j$},\ \ {\mathbb{E}}\langle\mathbf{v}_{i},\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle\langle\mathbf{v}_{j},\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle=0;\ \ \text{and for $i>0$},\ \ {\mathbb{E}}\lambda_{i}\langle\mathbf{v}_{i},\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle^{2}\eqsim i^{-b},\ \text{ for some $b>1$}.

A larger exponent bb implies a faster decay of signal 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} and thus corresponds to a simpler task (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007). Note that 1C satisfies Assumption 3 with b=ab=a.

Theorem 4.2 (Scaling law under source condition).

In Theorem 4.1, suppose Assumption 1C is replaced by Assumption 3 with 1<b<a+11<b<a+1. Then there exists some aa-dependent constant c>0c>0 such that when γ≤c\gamma\leq c, with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, we have

𝔼​ℛM​(𝐯N)=σ2+Θ⁡(1Mb−1)+Θ⁡(1(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)(b−1)/a)⏟𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑+𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌+Θ⁡(min⁡{M,(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a}N𝚎𝚏𝚏)⏟𝖵𝖺𝗋.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})=\sigma^{2}+\underbrace{\Theta\bigg(\frac{1}{M^{b-1}}\bigg)+\Theta\bigg(\frac{1}{(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{(b-1)/a}}\bigg)}_{\mathsf{Approx}+\mathsf{Bias}}+\underbrace{\Theta\bigg(\frac{\min\big\{M,\ (N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a}\big\}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}\bigg)}_{\mathsf{Var}}.

where the expectation is over the randomness of 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} and (𝐱i,yi)i=1N(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{N}, and Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) hides constants that may depend on (a,b)(a,b).

When 1<b≤a1<b\leq a, the tasks are relatively hard (compared to when b=ab=a), and the variance error is dominated by the sum of approximation and bias errors for all choices of MM, NN, and γ≲1\gamma\lesssim 1. In this case, Theorem 4.2 gives the same prediction about optimal stepsize and optimal allocation of data and model sizes under compute budget as Theorem 4.1.

When a<b<a+1a<b<a+1, the tasks are relatively easy (compared to when b=ab=a), and variance remains dominated by the sum of approximation and bias error if the stepsize is optimally tuned. Recall that γ≲1\gamma\lesssim 1, thus we can rewrite the risk bound in Theorem 4.2 as

𝔼​ℛM​(𝐯N)−σ2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})-\sigma^{2} ≂1min⁡{M,(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a}b−1+min⁡{M,(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a}N𝚎𝚏𝚏\displaystyle\eqsim\frac{1}{\min\big\{M,\ (N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a}\big\}^{b-1}}+\frac{\min\big\{M,\ (N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a}\big\}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}
≂{min⁡{M,(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a}/N𝚎𝚏𝚏M≳N𝚎𝚏𝚏1/b​and​N𝚎𝚏𝚏a/b−1≲γ≲1,min⁡{M,(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a}1−bM≲N𝚎𝚏𝚏1/b​or​γ≲N𝚎𝚏𝚏a/b−1.\displaystyle\eqsim\begin{cases}{\min\big\{M,\ (N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a}\big\}}/{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}&M\gtrsim N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{1/b}\ \text{and}\ N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{a/b-1}\lesssim\gamma\lesssim 1,\\ {\min\big\{M,\ (N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/a}\big\}^{1-b}}&M\lesssim N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{1/b}\ \text{or}\ \gamma\lesssim N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{a/b-1}.\end{cases}

Therefore the optimal stepsize and the risk under the optimal stepsize is

γ≂N𝚎𝚏𝚏a/b−1​ if ​M≳N𝚎𝚏𝚏1/b, and ​Ma/N𝚎𝚏𝚏≲γ≲1​ if ​M≲N𝚎𝚏𝚏1/b.\displaystyle\gamma\eqsim N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{a/b-1}\text{ if }M\gtrsim N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{1/b},~~~~~\text{ and }\ M^{a}/N_{\mathtt{eff}}\lesssim\gamma\lesssim 1\text{ if }M\lesssim N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{1/b}.

Under the optimally tunned stepsize, the population risk is in the form of

minγ⁡𝔼​ℛM​(𝐯N)=σ2+Θ⁡(N𝚎𝚏𝚏(1−b)/b)+Θ⁡(M1−b),\displaystyle\textstyle\min_{\gamma}\mathbb{E}\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})=\sigma^{2}+\Theta(N_{\mathtt{eff}}^{(1-b)/b})+\Theta(M^{1-b}),

which is again in the scaling law form Equation 1. This is expected since an optimally tuned stepsize controls the variance error by adjusting the strength of the implicit bias of SGD. Under a fixed compute budget C=M​NC=MN, our theory suggests to assign M=Θ~​(C1/(b+1))M=\tilde{\Theta}(C^{1/(b+1)}) and N=Θ~​(Cb/(b+1))N=\tilde{\Theta}(C^{b/(b+1)}), and set the stepsize to γ≂Θ~​(C(a−b)/(b+1))\gamma\eqsim\tilde{\Theta}(C^{(a-b)/(b+1)}).

When b≥a+1b\geq a+1, the tasks are even simpler. We provide upper and lower bounds in Appendix D.3. However, there exists a gap between the bounds, fixing which is left for future work.

Moreover, we note that in the comparable regimes where MM is large, the results in Theorem 4.2 match existing bounds on the risk of SGD iterates and ridge estimators (Pillaud-Vivien et al., 2018; Rudi and Rosasco, 2017).

4.2 Scaling law under logarithmic power law

We also derive the risk formula when the data covariance has a logarithmic power-law spectrum (Bartlett et al., 2020).

Assumption 4 (Logarithmic power-law spectrum).

There exists a>1a>1 such that the eigenvalues of 𝐇\mathbf{H} satisfy λi≂i−1​log−a⁡(i+1)\lambda_{i}\eqsim i^{-1}\log^{-a}(i+1), i>0i>0.

Theorem 4.3 (Scaling law under logarithmic power spectrum).

In Theorem 4.1, suppose Assumption 2 is replaced by Assumption 4. Then with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, we have

𝔼​ℛM​(𝐯N)=σ2+Θ⁡(1loga−1⁡(M))+Θ⁡(1loga−1⁡(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)),𝖵𝖺𝗋≂min⁡{M,N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γloga⁡(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)}N𝚎𝚏𝚏,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}_{N})=\sigma^{2}+\Theta\bigg(\frac{1}{\log^{a-1}(M)}\bigg)+\Theta\bigg(\frac{1}{\log^{a-1}(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)}\bigg),\quad\mathsf{Var}\eqsim\frac{\min\big\{M,\ \frac{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}{\log^{a}(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)}\big\}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}},

where the expectation is over the randomness of 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} and (𝐱i,yi)i=1N(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{N}.

Theorem 4.3 provides a scaling law under the logarithmic power-law spectrum. Similar to Theorem 4.1, the variance error is dominated by the approximation and bias errors for all choices of MM, NN, and γ\gamma, and thus disappeared from the risk bound. Different from Theorem 4.1, here the population risk is a polynomial of log⁡(M)\log(M) and log⁡(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)\log(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma).

5 Experiments

In this section, we examine the relation between the expected risk of the (SGD) output, the data size NN, and the model size MM when the covariates satisfy a power-law covariance spectrum. Although our results in Section 4 hold with high probability over 𝐒\mathbf{S}, for simplicity, we assume the expectation of the risk is taken over both 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} and 𝐒\mathbf{S} in our simulations. We adopt the model in Section 3 and train it using one-pass (SGD) with geometric decaying stepsize (3). We choose the dimension dd sufficiently large to approximate the infinite-dimensional case, and the data are generated so that Assumption 1 is satisfied. Moreover, we choose the covariance 𝐇∈ℝd×d\mathbf{H}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times d} to be diagonal with 𝐇i​i∝ia\mathbf{H}_{ii}\propto i^{a} and tr⁡(𝐇)=1\tr(\mathbf{H})=1 for some a>1.{a}>1. From Figure 1, we observe that the risk indeed follows a power-law formula jointly in the number of samples and the number of parameters. In addition, the fitted exponents are aligned with our theoretical predictions (a−1,1−1/a)(a-1,1-1/a) in Theorem 4.1. Figure 2 shows the scaling of the expected risk in data size (or model size) when the model size (or data size) is relatively large. We see that the expected risk also satisfies a power-law decay with exponents matching our predictions. It is noteworthy that our simulations demonstrate stronger observations than the theoretical results in Theorem 4.1, which only establishes matching upper and lower bounds up to a constant factor. Additional simulation results on the risk of the average of (SGD) iterates can be found in Appendix F.

6 Risk bounds under a general spectrum

In this section, we present some general results on the upper and lower bounds of the risk of the output of (SGD). Due to the rotational invariance of the sketched matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, without loss of generality, we assume the covariance 𝐇∈ℝd×d\mathbf{H}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times d} is diagonal with non-increasing diagonal entries. Our main results in Section 4 are directly built on the general bounds introduced here.

Assumption 5 (General distributional conditions).

Assume the following about the data distribution.

  1. A.

    Hypercontractivity.  There exists α≥1\alpha\geq 1 such that for every PSD matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} it holds that

    𝔼​𝐱𝐱⊤​𝐀𝐱𝐱⊤⪯α​tr⁡(𝐇𝐀)​𝐇.\mathbb{E}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\preceq\alpha\tr(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A})\mathbf{H}.
  2. B.

    Misspecified model.  There exists σ2>0\sigma^{2}>0 such that 𝔼​(y−𝐱⊤​𝐰∗)2​𝐱𝐱⊤⪯σ2​𝐇\mathbb{E}(y-\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{w}^{*})^{2}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\preceq\sigma^{2}\mathbf{H}.

It is clear that Assumption 1 implies Assumption 5 with α=3\alpha=3.

Excess risk decomposition.

Conditioning on the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, the training of the sketched linear predictor can be viewed as an MM-dimensional linear regression problem. We can therefore invoke existing SGD analysis (Wu et al., 2022a; Wu et al., 2022b) to sharply control the excess risk by controlling the bias and variance errors. Specifically, let us define the (𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*}-dependent) bias error as

𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗):=‖∏t=1N(𝐈−γt​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)​𝐯∗‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2,where​𝐯∗:=(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇𝐰∗,\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}):=\bigg\|\prod_{t=1}^{N}\big(\mathbf{I}-\gamma_{t}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big){\mathbf{v}^{*}}\bigg\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}},\quad\text{where}\ \mathbf{v}^{*}:=(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}^{*}, (5)

and the variance error as

𝖵𝖺𝗋:=#{λ~j≥1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏γ)}+(N𝚎𝚏𝚏γ)2∑λ~j<1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)λ~j2N𝚎𝚏𝚏,N𝚎𝚏𝚏:=N/log⁡(N),\mathsf{Var}:=\frac{\#\{\tilde{\lambda}_{j}\geq 1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)\}+(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{2}\sum_{\tilde{\lambda}_{j}<1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)}\tilde{\lambda}_{j}^{2}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}},\quad N_{\mathtt{eff}}:=N/\log(N), (6)

where (λ~j)j=1M\big(\tilde{\lambda}_{j}\big)_{j=1}^{M} are eigenvalues of 𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}. We also let 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌:=𝔼​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)\mathsf{Bias}:={\mathbb{E}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}), where the expectation is over the prior of 𝐰∗.\mathbf{w}^{*}. Using the existing results on the output of (SGD) in Wu et al. (2022a); Wu et al. (2022b), we show that the excess risk in (4) can be exactly decomposed as the sum of bias and variance errors under weak conditions.

Theorem 6.1 (Excess risk decomposition).

Conditioning on the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, consider the excess risk in Equation 4 induced by the output of Equation SGD. Assume 𝐯0=0\mathbf{v}_{0}=0. Then for any 𝐰∗∈ℍ\mathbf{w}^{*}\in\mathbb{H},

  1. 1.

    Under 5A and 5B and suppose γ≤1/(c​α​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤))\gamma\leq{1}/{\big(c\alpha\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})\big)} for some constant c>0c>0, we have

    𝔼​𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌≲𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗)+(α​‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2+σ2)​𝖵𝖺𝗋.\mathbb{E}\mathsf{Excess}\lesssim\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})+\big(\alpha\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}+\sigma^{2}\big)\mathsf{Var}.\vskip-3.00003pt
  2. 2.

    Under the stronger 1A and 1B and suppose γ≤1/(c​α​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤))\gamma\leq{1}/{\big(c\alpha\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}))} for some constant c>0c>0, we have

    𝔼​𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌≳𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗)+σ2​𝖵𝖺𝗋.\mathbb{E}\mathsf{Excess}\gtrsim\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})+\sigma^{2}\mathsf{Var}.

In both results, the expectations of 𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Excess} are taken over (𝐱t,yt)t=1N(\mathbf{x}_{t},y_{t})_{t=1}^{N}.

Assuming that the signal-to-noise ratio is upper bounded, that is, ‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2/σ2≲1\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}/\sigma^{2}\lesssim 1, then the bias-variance decomposition of the excess risk is sharp up to constant factors.

The variance error is in a nice form and can be computed using the following important lemma on the spectrum of 𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}. Similar results for logarithmic power-law are also established in Lemma G.6 in Appendix G.

Lemma 6.2 (Power law).

Under Assumption 2, it holds with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} that

μj(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)≂μj(𝐇)≂j−a,j=1,…,M.\displaystyle\mu_{j}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})\eqsim\mu_{j}(\mathbf{H})\eqsim j^{-a},\quad j=1,\dots,M.

For any 0≤k∗≤k†≤∞0\leq k^{*}\leq k^{\dagger}\leq\infty, let 𝐒k∗:k†∈ℝM×(k†−k∗)\mathbf{S}_{k^{*}:k^{\dagger}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{M\times(k^{\dagger}-k^{*})} denote the matrix formed by the k∗+1−k†k^{*}+1-k^{\dagger}-th columns of 𝐒\mathbf{S}. We also abuse the notation k†:∞k^{\dagger}:\infty for k†:dk^{\dagger}:d when dd is finite. We let 𝐇k∗:k†∈ℝ(k†−k∗)×(k†−k∗)\mathbf{H}_{k^{*}:k^{\dagger}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{(k^{\dagger}-k^{*})\times(k^{\dagger}-k^{*})} be the submatrix of 𝐇\mathbf{H} formed by the k∗+1−k†k^{*}+1-k^{\dagger}-th eigenvalues. For the approximation and bias error, we use the following upper and lower bounds to compute their values.

Theorem 6.3 (A general upper bound).

Suppose Assumption 5 holds. 7 Conclusion

We analyze neural scaling laws in infinite-dimensional linear regression. We consider a linear predictor with MM trainable parameters on the sketched covariates, which is trained by one-pass stochastic gradient descent with NN data. Under a Gaussian prior assumption on the optimal model parameter and a power law (of degree a>1a>1) assumption on the spectrum of the data covariance, we derive matching upper and lower bounds on the population risk minus the irreducible error, that is, Θ(M−(a−1)+N−(a−1)/a)\Theta(M^{-(a-1)}+N^{-(a-1)/a}). In particular, we show that the variance error, which increases with MM, is of strictly higher order compared to the other errors, thus disappearing from the risk bound. We attribute the nice empirical formula of the neural scaling law to the non-domination of the variance error, which ultimately is an effect of the implicit regularization of SGD.

Many directions remain open for future study. First, our work is limited to the linear model; it would be interesting to see whether similar scaling laws can be derived in more complex models, such as random feature models or two-layer networks. Second, we focus on one-pass SGD training, and it is unclear if similar results hold for other optimization methods like accelerated SGD or Adam. Additionally, from a technical perspective, many results in our work depend on the Gaussian assumption and the source condition of the data. Investigating how these assumptions can be relaxed would also be valuable.

A.1 Additional notations and comments on data assumptions

Tensors.

For matrices 𝐀\mathbf{A}, 𝐁\mathbf{B}, 𝐂\mathbf{C}, 𝐃\mathbf{D}, and 𝐗\mathbf{X} of appropriate shape, it holds that

(𝐁⊤⊗𝐀)∘𝐗=𝐀𝐗𝐁,(\mathbf{B}^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{A})\circ\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B},

(𝐃⊤⊗𝐂)∘(𝐁⊤⊗𝐀)∘𝐗\displaystyle(\mathbf{D}^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{C})\circ(\mathbf{B}^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{A})\circ\mathbf{X} =((𝐃⊤​𝐁⊤)⊗(𝐂𝐀))∘𝐗\displaystyle=\big((\mathbf{D}^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{\top})\otimes(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A})\big)\circ\mathbf{X}
=𝐂𝐀𝐗𝐁𝐃.\displaystyle=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D}.

𝐀⊗2:=𝐀⊗𝐀.\mathbf{A}^{\otimes 2}:=\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{A}.
Comments on Assumption 2, 3 and 4

Due to the rotational invariance of the Gaussian sketched matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, throughout the appendix, we assume w.l.o.g. that the covariance of the input covariates 𝐇\mathbf{H} is diagonal with the (i,i)(i,i)-th entry being the ii-th eigenvalue. Specifically, Assumption 3 can be rewritten as

Assumption 6 (Source condition).

Assume 𝐇=(hi​j)i,j≥1\mathbf{H}=(h_{ij})_{i,j\geq 1} is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries in non-increasing order, and 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} satisfies a prior such that

for i≠j,𝔼​𝐰i∗​𝐰j∗=0;and for i>0,𝔼​λi​𝐰i∗2≂i−b, for some b>1.\text{for $i\neq j$},\ \ {\mathbb{E}}\mathbf{w}^{*}_{i}\mathbf{w}^{*}_{j}=0;\ \ \text{and for $i>0$},\ \ {\mathbb{E}}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{w}_{i}^{*2}\eqsim i^{-b},\ \text{ for some $b>1$}.

Now that we assume 𝐇\mathbf{H} is diagonal. We make the following notations. Define

𝐇k∗:k†:=diag(λk∗+1,…,λk†)∈ℝ(k†−k∗)2,\mathbf{H}_{k^{*}:k^{\dagger}}:=\diag(\lambda_{k^{*}+1},\dots,\lambda_{k^{\dagger}})\in\mathbb{R}^{(k^{\dagger}-k^{*})^{2}},

where 0≤k∗≤k†0\leq k^{*}\leq k^{\dagger} are two integers, and we allow k†=∞k^{\dagger}=\infty. For example,

Conditional on the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, the minimizer of ℛM​(𝐯)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}) is given by

=‖(𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12)​𝐇12​𝐰∗‖2.\displaystyle=\Big\|\Big(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big)\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\Big\|^{2}. (7)

Proof of Lemma A.1.

Recall that the risk

ℛ⁡(𝐰):=𝔼​(⟨𝐱,𝐰⟩−y)2\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}):=\mathbb{E}\big(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}\rangle-y\big)^{2}

is a quadratic function and that 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} is the minimizer of ℛ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{R}(\cdot), so we have

(𝔼​𝐱⊗2)​𝐰∗=𝔼​𝐱​y⇔𝐇𝐰∗=𝔼​𝐱​y,\displaystyle\big(\mathbb{E}\mathbf{x}^{\otimes 2}\big)\mathbf{w}^{*}=\mathbb{E}\mathbf{x}y\Leftrightarrow\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}^{*}=\mathbb{E}\mathbf{x}y,

and

ℛ⁡(𝐰)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}) =𝔼​(⟨𝐱,𝐰⟩−⟨𝐱,𝐰∗⟩)2+ℛ⁡(𝐰∗)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\big(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}\rangle-\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle\big)^{2}+\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}^{*})
=‖𝐇12​(𝐰−𝐰∗)‖2+ℛ⁡(𝐰∗).\displaystyle=\|\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^{*})\|^{2}+\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

Recall that the risk in a restricted subspace

ℛM​(𝐯):=ℛ⁡(𝐒⊤​𝐯)=𝔼​(⟨𝐒𝐱,𝐯⟩−y)2\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}):=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v})=\mathbb{E}\big(\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}\rangle-y\big)^{2}

𝐯∗\displaystyle{\mathbf{v}^{*}} =(𝔼​(𝐒𝐱)⊗2)−1​𝔼​𝐒𝐱​y\displaystyle=\big(\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x})^{\otimes 2}\big)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}y
=(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇𝐰∗.\displaystyle=\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}{\mathbf{w}^{*}}.

Therefore, the approximation error is

𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle\mathsf{Approx} :=ℛM​(𝐯∗)−ℛ⁡(𝐰∗)\displaystyle:=\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}^{*})-\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}^{*})
=ℛ⁡(𝐒⊤​𝐯∗)−ℛ⁡(𝐰∗)\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*})-\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}^{*})
=‖𝐇12​(𝐒⊤​𝐯∗−𝐰∗)‖2\displaystyle=\|\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*}-\mathbf{w}^{*})\|^{2}
=‖𝐇12​(𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇𝐰∗−𝐰∗)‖2\displaystyle=\|\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}{\mathbf{w}^{*}}-\mathbf{w}^{*})\|^{2}
=‖(𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12)​𝐇12​𝐰∗‖2.\displaystyle=\Big\|\Big(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big)\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\Big\|^{2}.

Finally, since

(𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12)2=𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12⪯𝐈,\displaystyle\Big(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big)^{2}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\preceq\mathbf{I},

it follows that 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≤‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2\mathsf{Approx}\leq\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}. ∎

A.3 Bias-variance decomposition

The excess risk in Equation 4 can be viewed as the SGD excess risk in an MM-dimensional (misspecified) linear regression problem. We will utilize Corollary 3.4 in (Wu et al., 2022b) to get a bias-variance decomposition of the excess risk. The following two lemmas check the related assumptions for Corollary 3.4 in (Wu et al., 2022b) in our setup.

Lemma A.2 (Hypercontractivity and the misspecified noise under sketched feature).

Suppose that 5A and 5B hold. Conditioning on the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, for every PSD matrix 𝐀∈ℝM×M\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}, we have

𝔼​(𝐒𝐱)⊗2​𝐀​(𝐒𝐱)⊗2⪯α​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤​𝐀)​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x})^{\otimes 2}\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x})^{\otimes 2}\preceq\alpha\tr\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\big)\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}.

Moreover, for the minimizer of ℛM​(𝐯)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}), that is, 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*} defined in Lemma A.1, we have

𝔼​(y−⟨𝐯∗,𝐒𝐱⟩)2​(𝐒𝐱)⊗2⪯2​(σ2+α​‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2)​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big(y-\langle\mathbf{v}^{*},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}\rangle\big)^{2}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x})^{\otimes 2}\preceq 2(\sigma^{2}+\alpha\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}})\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}.

The expectation in the above is over (𝐱,y)(\mathbf{x},y).

Proof of Lemma A.2.

The first part is a direct application of 5A:

𝔼​(𝐒𝐱)⊗2​𝐀​(𝐒𝐱)⊗2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x})^{\otimes 2}\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x})^{\otimes 2} =𝐒⁡(𝔼​𝐱𝐱⊤​(𝐒⊤​𝐀𝐒)​𝐱𝐱⊤)​𝐒⊤\displaystyle=\mathbf{S}\big(\mathbb{E}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{S})\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\big)\mathbf{S}^{\top}
⪯𝐒⁡(α​tr⁡(𝐇𝐒⊤​𝐀𝐒)​𝐇)​𝐒⊤\displaystyle\preceq\mathbf{S}\big(\alpha\tr\big(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{S}\big)\mathbf{H}\big)\mathbf{S}^{\top}
=α​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤​𝐀)​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤.\displaystyle=\alpha\tr\big(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\big)\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}.

For the second part, we first show that

𝔼​(y−⟨𝐯∗,𝐒𝐱⟩)2​𝐱⊗2\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}\big(y-\langle\mathbf{v}^{*},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}\rangle\big)^{2}\mathbf{x}^{\otimes 2}} ⪯2​𝔼​(y−⟨𝐰∗,𝐱⟩)2​𝐱⊗2+2​𝔼​⟨𝐰∗−𝐒⊤​𝐯∗,𝐱⟩2​𝐱⊗2\displaystyle\preceq 2\mathbb{E}\big(y-\langle\mathbf{w}^{*},\mathbf{x}\rangle\big)^{2}\mathbf{x}^{\otimes 2}+2\mathbb{E}\langle\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*},\mathbf{x}\rangle^{2}\mathbf{x}^{\otimes 2}
⪯2​σ2​𝐇+2​α​⟨𝐇,(𝐰∗−𝐒⊤​𝐯∗)⊗2⟩​𝐇,\displaystyle\preceq 2\sigma^{2}\mathbf{H}+2\alpha\langle\mathbf{H},(\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*})^{\otimes 2}\rangle\mathbf{H},

where the last inequality is by 5A and 5B. From the proof of Lemma A.1, we know that

⟨𝐇,(𝐰∗−𝐒⊤​𝐯∗)⊗2⟩=𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≤‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2,almost surely.\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{H},(\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*})^{\otimes 2}\rangle=\mathsf{Approx}\leq\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}},\ \text{almost surely}.

So we have

𝔼​(y−⟨𝐯∗,𝐒𝐱⟩)2​𝐱⊗2⪯2​(σ2+α​‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2)​𝐇.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big(y-\langle\mathbf{v}^{*},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}\rangle\big)^{2}\mathbf{x}^{\otimes 2}\preceq 2(\sigma^{2}+\alpha\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}})\mathbf{H}.

Left and right multiplying both sides with 𝐒\mathbf{S} and 𝐒⊤\mathbf{S}^{\top}, we obtain the second claim. ∎

Lemma A.3 (Gaussianity and well-specified noise under sketched features).

Suppose that 1A and 1B hold. Conditional on the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, we have

𝐒𝐱∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤).\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}).

Moreover, for the minimizer of ℛM​(𝐯)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathbf{v}), that is, 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*} defined in Lemma A.1, we have

𝔼⁡[y|𝐒𝐱]=⟨𝐒𝐱,𝐯∗⟩,𝔼​(y−⟨𝐒𝐱,𝐯∗⟩)2=σ2+𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≥σ2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[y|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}]=\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle,\quad\mathbb{E}(y-\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle)^{2}=\sigma^{2}+\mathsf{Approx}\geq\sigma^{2}.
Proof of Lemma A.3.

The first claim is a direct consequence of 1A.

For the second claim, by 1A and Lemma A.1, we have

𝔼⁡[y|𝐱]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[y|\mathbf{x}] =⟨𝐱,𝐰∗⟩\displaystyle=\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle
=⟨𝐱,𝐒⊤​𝐯∗⟩+⟨𝐱,𝐰∗−𝐒⊤​𝐯∗⟩\displaystyle=\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle
=⟨𝐱,𝐒⊤​𝐯∗⟩+⟨𝐱,[𝐈−(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇]​𝐰∗⟩\displaystyle=\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{x},\big[\mathbf{I}-(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\big]\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle
=⟨𝐇−12​𝐱,𝐇12​𝐒⊤​𝐯∗⟩+⟨𝐇−12​𝐱,[𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12]​𝐇12​𝐰∗⟩\displaystyle=\langle\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x},\big[\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\big]\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle
=⟨𝐒𝐇12​𝐇−12​𝐱,𝐯∗⟩+⟨[𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12]​𝐇−12​𝐱,𝐇12​𝐰∗⟩.\displaystyle=\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle+\langle\big[\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\big]\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle. (8)

Notice that

𝐇−12​𝐱∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈),\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}),

by 1A and that

𝐒𝐇12​[𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12]=0,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\big[\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\big]=0,

therefore

𝐒𝐱=𝐒𝐇12​𝐇−12​𝐱​is independent of​[𝐈−𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇12]​𝐇−12​𝐱.\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x}\ \text{is independent of}\ \big[\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\big]\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x}.

Taking expectation over the second random vector in Equation 8, we find

𝔼⁡[y|𝐒𝐱]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[y|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}] =𝔼​𝔼​[y|𝐱]=⟨𝐒𝐇12​𝐇−12​𝐱,𝐯∗⟩=⟨𝐒𝐱,𝐯∗⟩.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\mathbb{E}[y|\mathbf{x}]=\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle=\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle.

It remains to show

𝔼​(y−⟨𝐒𝐱,𝐯∗⟩)2=σ2+𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑.\mathbb{E}(y-\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle)^{2}=\sigma^{2}+\mathsf{Approx}.

This follows from the proof of Lemma A.1. Specifically,

𝔼​(y−⟨𝐒𝐱,𝐯∗⟩)2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(y-\langle\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}^{*}\rangle)^{2} =ℛ⁡(𝐒⊤​𝐯∗)\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*})
=𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑+ℛ⁡(𝐰∗)\displaystyle=\mathsf{Approx}+\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}^{*})

≥σ2,\displaystyle\geq\sigma^{2},

where the second equality is by the definition of 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\mathsf{Approx} and the third equality is by 1B. We have completed the proof. ∎

A.4 Proof of Theorem 6.1

We now use the results in (Wu et al., 2022a; Wu et al., 2022b) for SGD to obtain the following bias-variance decomposition on the excess risk.

Theorem A.4 (Excess risk bounds).

Consider the excess risk in Equation 4 induced by the output of Equation SGD. Let

N𝚎𝚏𝚏:=N/log⁡(N),𝚂𝙽𝚁:=(‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2+‖𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2)/σ2.N_{\mathtt{eff}}:=N/\log(N),\quad\mathtt{SNR}:=(\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}+\|\mathbf{v}_{0}\|_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}^{2})/\sigma^{2}.

Then conditioning on the sketch matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, for any 𝐰∗∈ℍ\mathbf{w}^{*}\in\mathbb{H}

  • 2.

    Under 1A and 1B, we have

    𝔼​𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌≳‖∏t=1N(𝐈−γt​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)​(𝐯0−𝐯∗)‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2+σ2⋅D𝚎𝚏𝚏N𝚎𝚏𝚏\mathbb{E}\mathsf{Excess}\gtrsim\bigg\|\prod_{t=1}^{N}\big(\mathbf{I}-\gamma_{t}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)(\mathbf{v}_{0}-{\mathbf{v}^{*}})\bigg\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}+\sigma^{2}\cdot\frac{D_{\mathtt{eff}}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}

D𝚎𝚏𝚏:=#{λ~j≥1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏γ)}+(N𝚎𝚏𝚏γ)2∑λ~j<1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)λ~j2,\displaystyle D_{\mathtt{eff}}:=\#\{\tilde{\lambda}_{j}\geq 1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)\}+(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{2}\sum_{\tilde{\lambda}_{j}<1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)}\tilde{\lambda}_{j}^{2},

Theorem 6.1 follows immediately by Lemma A.1 and by setting 𝐯0=0\mathbf{v}_{0}=0 and plugging the definition of 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗)\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) and 𝖵𝖺𝗋\mathsf{Var} into Theorem A.4.

Proof of Theorem A.4.

This follows from Corollary 3.4 in (Wu et al., 2022b) for a linear regression problem with population data given by (𝐒𝐱,y)(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x},y). Note that the data covariance becomes 𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top} and the optimal model parameter becomes 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*}.

For the upper bound, Lemma A.2 verifies Assumptions 1A and 2 in (Wu et al., 2022b), with the noise level being

σ~2=2​(σ2+α​‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2).\tilde{\sigma}^{2}=2(\sigma^{2}+\alpha\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}).

Then we can apply the upper bound in Corollary 3.4 in (Wu et al., 2022b) (setting their index set 𝕂=∅\mathbb{K}=\emptyset) to get

𝔼​𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌≲‖∏t=1N(𝐈−γt​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)​(𝐯0−𝐯∗)‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2+(‖𝐯∗−𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2+σ~2)​D𝚎𝚏𝚏N𝚎𝚏𝚏.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathsf{Excess}\lesssim\bigg\|\prod_{t=1}^{N}\big(\mathbf{I}-\gamma_{t}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)(\mathbf{v}_{0}-{\mathbf{v}^{*}})\bigg\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}+(\|\mathbf{v}^{*}-\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}+\tilde{\sigma}^{2})\frac{D_{\mathtt{eff}}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}.

We verify that

‖𝐯∗−𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2\displaystyle\|\mathbf{v}^{*}-\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}} ≤2​‖𝐇12​𝐒⊤​𝐯∗‖2+2​‖𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2\displaystyle\leq 2\|\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{*}\|^{2}+2\|\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}
=2​‖𝐇12​𝐒⊤​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)−1​𝐒𝐇𝐰∗‖2+2​‖𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2\displaystyle=2\|\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{S}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}+2\|\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}
≤2​‖𝐇12​𝐰∗‖2+2​‖𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2\displaystyle\leq 2\|\mathbf{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}+2\|\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}
=2​‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2+2​‖𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2,\displaystyle=2\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}+2\|\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}},

which implies that

(‖𝐯∗−𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2+σ~2)\displaystyle(\|\mathbf{v}^{*}-\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}+\tilde{\sigma}^{2}) ≤2​‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2+2​‖𝐯0‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2+2​(σ2+α​‖𝐰∗‖𝐇2)\displaystyle\leq 2\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}}+2\|\mathbf{v}_{0}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}+2(\sigma^{2}+\alpha\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}})
≲(1+α​𝚂𝙽𝚁)​σ2.\displaystyle\lesssim(1+\alpha\mathtt{SNR})\sigma^{2}.

Substituting, we get the upper bound.

For the lower bound, Lemma A.3 shows 𝐒𝐱\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x} is Gaussian, therefore it satisfies Assumption 1B in Wu et al. (2022b) with β=1\beta=1. Besides, Lemma A.3 shows that the linear regression problem is well-specified, with the noise level being

σ~2=σ2+𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≥σ2.\tilde{\sigma}^{2}=\sigma^{2}+\mathsf{Approx}\geq\sigma^{2}.

Although the lower bound in Corollary 3.4 in Wu et al. (2022b) is stated for Gaussian additive noise (see their Assumption 2’), it is easy to check that the lower bound holds for any well-specified noise as described by Lemma A.3. Using the lower bound in Corollary 3.4 in Wu et al. (2022b), we obtain

𝔼​𝖤𝗑𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌≳‖∏t=1N(𝐈−γt​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)​(𝐯0−𝐯∗)‖𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤2+σ~2​D𝚎𝚏𝚏N𝚎𝚏𝚏.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathsf{Excess}\gtrsim\bigg\|\prod_{t=1}^{N}\big(\mathbf{I}-\gamma_{t}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\big)(\mathbf{v}_{0}-{\mathbf{v}^{*}})\bigg\|^{2}_{\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}}+\tilde{\sigma}^{2}\frac{D_{\mathtt{eff}}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}}.

Plugging in σ~2≥σ2\tilde{\sigma}^{2}\geq\sigma^{2} gives the desired lower bound. ∎

A.5 Proofs of Lemma 6.2, Theorem 6.3 and 6.4

Lemma 6.2 is proved in Lemma G.4. Theorem 6.3 follows from Lemma C.1 and D.1. Theorem 6.4 follows from Lemma C.2 and D.2.

Appendix B Proofs in Section 4

B.1 Proof of Theorem 4.1

Proof of part 1.

By Assumption 1B and the definition of ℛ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{R}(\cdot), we have

ℛ⁡(𝐰)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}) =𝔼​(⟨𝐱,𝐰⟩−y)2=𝔼​(⟨𝐱,𝐰⟩−𝔼⁡[y∣𝐱])2+𝔼​(y−𝔼⁡[y∣𝐱])2\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}\rangle-y)^{2}={\mathbb{E}}(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}\rangle-{\mathbb{E}}[y\mid\mathbf{x}])^{2}+{\mathbb{E}}(y-{\mathbb{E}}[y\mid\mathbf{x}])^{2}
=𝔼​(⟨𝐱,𝐰⟩−⟨𝐱,𝐰∗⟩)2+σ2≥σ2.\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}\rangle-\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}^{*}\rangle)^{2}+\sigma^{2}\geq\sigma^{2}.

Note that the equality holds if and only if 𝐰=𝐰∗.\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}^{*}. Therefore we have min⁡ℛ⁡(⋅)=ℛ⁡(𝐰∗)=σ2.\min\mathcal{R}(\cdot)=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{w}^{*})=\sigma^{2}.

Proof of part 2.

Part 2 of Theorem 4.1 follows immediately from Lemma C.2.

Proof of part 3.

Appendix C Approximation error

In this section, we derive upper and lower bounds for the approximation error in (4) (and 7). We will also show that the upper and lower bounds match up to constant factors in several examples.

C.1 An upper bound

Lemma C.1 (An upper bound on the approximation error).

Given any k≤dk\leq d such that r⁡(𝐇)≥k+Mr(\mathbf{H})\geq k+M, the approximation error in (4) (and 7) satisfies

𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≲∥𝐰k:∞∗∥𝐇k:∞2+⟨[𝐇0:k−1+𝐒0:k⊤𝐀k−1𝐒0:k]−1,𝐰0:k∗𝐰0:k∗⊤⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Approx}\lesssim\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k:\infty}}}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}_{{k:\infty}}}+\langle[\mathbf{H}_{{0:k}}^{-1}+\mathbf{S}_{{0:k}}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{0:k}}]^{-1},{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}^{\top}\rangle

almost surely, where 𝐀k:=𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐒k:∞⊤\mathbf{A}_{k}:=\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}^{\top}. If in addition k≤M/2k\leq M/2, then with probability 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}

𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≲∥𝐰k:∞∗∥𝐇k:∞2+(∑i>kλiM+λk+1+∑i>kλi2M)∥𝐰0:k∗∥2,\displaystyle\mathsf{Approx}\lesssim\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k:\infty}}}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}_{{k:\infty}}}+\Big(\frac{\sum_{i>k}\lambda_{i}}{M}+\lambda_{k+1}+\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i>k}\lambda_{i}^{2}}{M}}\Big)\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}\|^{2},

+2𝔼𝐰∗⟨𝖴𝖵+𝖵𝖶,𝐇0:k1/2𝐰0:k∗𝐰k:∞∗𝐇k:∞1/2⟩\displaystyle\quad+2\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\big\langle{\mathsf{U}}{\mathsf{V}}+{\mathsf{V}}{\mathsf{W}},\mathbf{H}_{0:k}^{1/2}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k:\infty}}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}^{1/2}\big\rangle
=tr((𝖴2+𝖵𝖵⊤)𝐇0:k)+tr((𝖶2+𝖵⊤𝖵)𝐇k:∞),\displaystyle=\tr(({\mathsf{U}}^{2}+{\mathsf{V}}{\mathsf{V}}^{\top})\mathbf{H}_{0:k})+\tr(({\mathsf{W}}^{2}+{\mathsf{V}}^{\top}{\mathsf{V}})\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}),

where the last line uses the fact that 𝔼𝐰∗​(𝐰∗)⊗2=𝐈d.\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}(\mathbf{w}^{*})^{\otimes 2}=\mathbf{I}_{d}. Using Eq. (13) and (16) in the proof of Lemma C.1, we further obtain

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Approx} =tr(𝐇0:k−1/2[𝐇0:k−1+𝐒0:k⊤𝐀k−1𝐒0:k]−1𝐇0:k−1/2𝐇0:k)−tr(𝖶𝐇k:∞)\displaystyle=\tr(\mathbf{H}^{-1/2}_{{0:k}}[\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{{0:k}}+\mathbf{S}^{\top}_{{0:k}}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{0:k}}]^{-1}\mathbf{H}^{-1/2}_{{0:k}}\mathbf{H}_{0:k})-\tr({\mathsf{W}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty})
=tr([𝐇0:k−1+𝐒0:k⊤𝐀k−1𝐒0:k]−1)−tr(𝖶𝐇k:∞)\displaystyle=\tr([\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{{0:k}}+\mathbf{S}^{\top}_{{0:k}}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{0:k}}]^{-1})-\tr({\mathsf{W}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty})
≥−tr(𝖶𝐇k:∞)=:T3.\displaystyle\geq-\tr({\mathsf{W}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty})=:T_{3}.

where 𝐀k:=𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐒k:∞⊤.\mathbf{A}_{k}:=\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}\mathbf{S}_{k:\infty}^{\top}. For T3T_{3}, we further have

T3\displaystyle T_{3} =tr(𝐇k:∞1/2[𝐈d−k−𝐇k:∞1/2𝐒k:∞⊤𝐀−1𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞1/2]𝐇k:∞1/2)\displaystyle=\tr(\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}^{1/2}[\mathbf{I}_{d-k}-\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}}]\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}^{1/2})
≥tr(𝐇k:∞1/2[𝐈d−k−𝐇k:∞1/2𝐒k:∞⊤𝐀k−1𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞1/2]𝐇k:∞1/2)\displaystyle\geq\tr(\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}^{1/2}[\mathbf{I}_{d-k}-\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}}]\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}^{1/2})
≥∑i=1d−kμi(𝐈d−k−𝐇k:∞1/2𝐒k:∞⊤𝐀k−1𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞1/2)⋅μd+1−k−i(𝐇k:∞),\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i=1}^{d-k}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{I}_{d-k}-\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}})\cdot\mu_{d+1-k-i}(\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}),

where the second line is due to 𝐀⪰𝐀k\mathbf{A}\succeq\mathbf{A}_{k} (and hence −𝐀−1⪰−𝐀k−1-\mathbf{A}^{-1}\succeq-\mathbf{A}^{-1}_{k} ), the third line follows from Von-Neuman’s inequality. Since 𝐌:=𝐈d−k−𝐇1/2k:∞𝐒k:∞⊤𝐀k−1𝐒k:∞𝐇1/2k:∞\mathbf{M}:=\mathbf{I}_{d-k}-\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}} is a projection matrix such that 𝐌2=𝐌\mathbf{M}^{2}=\mathbf{M} and tr⁡(𝐈d−k−𝐌)=M\tr(\mathbf{I}_{d-k}-\mathbf{M})=M, it follows that 𝐌\mathbf{M} has MM eigenvalues 00 and d−k−Md-k-M eigenvalues 11. T3\displaystyle T_{3} ≥∑i=1d−kμi(𝐌)⋅μd+1−k−i(𝐇k:∞)≥∑i=k+Mdλi\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i=1}^{d-k}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{M})\cdot\mu_{d+1-k-i}(\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty})\geq\sum_{i=k+M}^{d}\lambda_{i}

for any k≤dk\leq d. Letting k=0k=0 maximizes the lower bound and concludes the proof. ∎

C.3 A lower bound under Assumption 3

Lemma C.3 (Lower bound on the approximation error under Assumption 3).

Under Assumption 3, the approximation error in (4) (and 7) satisfies

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≳∑i=Mdλi​ia−b,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Approx}\gtrsim\sum_{i=M}^{d}\lambda_{i}i^{a-b},

where (λi)i=1d(\lambda_{i})_{i=1}^{d} are eigenvalues of 𝐇\mathbf{H} in non-increasing order and the inequality hides some (a,b)(a,b)-dependent constant.

Proof of Lemma C.3.

The proof is essentially the same as the proof of Lemma C.2 but we include it here for completeness. Let 𝐇𝐰:=𝔼⁡[𝐰∗​𝐰∗⁣⊤]\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}:={\mathbb{E}}[\mathbf{w}^{*}\mathbf{w}^{*\top}] be the covariance of the prior on 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*}. Following the proof of Lemma C.2, we have

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Approx} =𝔼𝐰∗⟨𝖴2+𝖵𝖵⊤,𝐇0:k1/2𝐰0:k∗𝐰0:k∗𝐇0:k1/2⟩+𝔼𝐰∗⟨𝖶2+𝖵⊤𝖵,𝐇0:k1/2𝐰k:∞∗𝐰k:∞∗𝐇k:∞1/2⟩\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\big\langle{\mathsf{U}}^{2}+{\mathsf{V}}{\mathsf{V}}^{\top},\mathbf{H}_{0:k}^{1/2}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}\mathbf{H}_{0:k}^{1/2}\big\rangle+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\big\langle{\mathsf{W}}^{2}+{\mathsf{V}}^{\top}{\mathsf{V}},\mathbf{H}_{0:k}^{1/2}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k:\infty}}}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k:\infty}}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}^{1/2}\big\rangle
+2𝔼𝐰∗⟨𝖴𝖵+𝖵𝖶,𝐇0:k1/2𝐰0:k∗𝐰k:∞∗𝐇k:∞1/2⟩\displaystyle\quad+2\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\big\langle{\mathsf{U}}{\mathsf{V}}+{\mathsf{V}}{\mathsf{W}},\mathbf{H}_{0:k}^{1/2}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k:\infty}}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}^{1/2}\big\rangle
=tr((𝖴2+𝖵𝖵⊤)𝐇0:k𝐇0:k𝐰)+tr((𝖶2+𝖵⊤𝖵)𝐇k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐰),\displaystyle=\tr(({\mathsf{U}}^{2}+{\mathsf{V}}{\mathsf{V}}^{\top})\mathbf{H}_{0:k}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{0:k})+\tr(({\mathsf{W}}^{2}+{\mathsf{V}}^{\top}{\mathsf{V}})\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{k:\infty}),

where the last line uses Assumption 3 and notice that 𝐇,𝐇𝐰\mathbf{H},\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}} are both diagonal. Next, similar to the proof of Lemma C.2, using Eq. (13) and (16), we derive

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Approx} =tr(𝐇0:k−1/2[𝐇0:k−1+𝐒0:k⊤𝐀k−1𝐒0:k]−1𝐇0:k−1/2𝐇0:k𝐇0:k𝐰)−tr(𝖶𝐇k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐰)\displaystyle=\tr(\mathbf{H}^{-1/2}_{{0:k}}[\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{{0:k}}+\mathbf{S}^{\top}_{{0:k}}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{0:k}}]^{-1}\mathbf{H}^{-1/2}_{{0:k}}\mathbf{H}_{0:k}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{0:k})-\tr({\mathsf{W}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{k:\infty})
=tr([𝐇0:k−1+𝐒0:k⊤𝐀k−1𝐒0:k]−1𝐇0:k𝐰)−tr(𝖶𝐇k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐰)\displaystyle=\tr([\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{{0:k}}+\mathbf{S}^{\top}_{{0:k}}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{0:k}}]^{-1}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{0:k})-\tr({\mathsf{W}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{k:\infty})
≥−tr(𝖶𝐇k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐰)=:T~3\displaystyle\geq-\tr({\mathsf{W}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{k:\infty})=:{\tilde{T}}_{3}

where 𝐀k:=𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐒k:∞⊤\mathbf{A}_{k}:=\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}\mathbf{S}_{k:\infty}^{\top}. For T~3{\tilde{T}}_{3}, following the same argument for T3T_{3} in the proof of Lemma C.2, we have

T~3\displaystyle{\tilde{T}}_{3} ≥∑i=1d−kμi(𝐈d−k−𝐇k:∞1/2𝐒k:∞⊤𝐀k−1𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞1/2)⋅μd+1−k−i(𝐇k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐰)\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i=1}^{d-k}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{I}_{d-k}-\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{k}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}^{1/2}_{{k:\infty}})\cdot\mu_{d+1-k-i}(\mathbf{H}_{k:\infty}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}_{k:\infty})
≥∑i=k+Mdμi​(𝐇𝐇𝐰)≳∑i=k+Mdia−b​λi,\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i=k+M}^{d}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}})\gtrsim\sum_{i=k+M}^{d}i^{a-b}\lambda_{i},

for any k≤dk\leq d where the last inequality uses Assumption 3. Setting k=0k=0 maximizes the lower bound and concludes the proof. ∎

C.4 Examples on matching bounds for 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\mathsf{Approx}

In this section, we derive matching upper and lower bounds for 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\mathsf{Approx} (defined in Eq. 4 and 7) in three concrete examples: power-law spectrum (Lemma C.4), power-law spectrum with source condition (Lemma C.5) and logarithmic power-law spectrum (Lemma D.5).

Lemma C.4 (Bounds on 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\mathsf{Approx} under the power-law spectrum).

Suppose Assumption 1C and 2 hold. Then with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of 𝐒\mathbf{S}

M1−a≲𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≲M1−a.\displaystyle M^{1-a}\lesssim{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx}\lesssim M^{1-a}.

Here, the hidden constants only depend on the power-law degree a.a.

Proof of Lemma C.4.

For the upper bound, by Lemma C.1 and noting 𝔼​𝐰i∗2=1{\mathbb{E}}\mathbf{w}^{*2}_{i}=1 for all ii, we have with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx} ≲∑k>k1λi+(∑i>k1λiM+λk1+1+∑i>k1λi2M)⋅k1\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{k>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}+\bigg(\frac{\sum_{i>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}}{M}+\lambda_{k_{1}+1}+\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}^{2}}{M}}\bigg)\cdot k_{1}
≲k11−a+(k11−aM+k1−a+k11−2​aM)​k1\displaystyle\lesssim k_{1}^{1-a}+\bigg(\frac{k_{1}^{1-a}}{M}+k_{1}^{-a}+\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}^{1-2a}}{M}}\bigg)k_{1}
≲(k1M+1)​k11−a\displaystyle\lesssim\bigg(\frac{k_{1}}{M}+1\bigg)k_{1}^{1-a}

for any given k1≤M/2k_{1}\leq M/2. Here the hidden constants depend on aa. Therefore, letting k1=M/2k_{1}=M/2 in the upper bound yields

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx} ≲M1−a\displaystyle\lesssim M^{1-{a}}

with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}.

For the lower bound, we have from Lemma C.2 that

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≳∑i=M∞i−a≳M1−a.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Approx}\gtrsim\sum_{i=M}^{\infty}i^{-a}\gtrsim M^{1-{a}}.

This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma C.5 (Bounds on 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\mathsf{Approx} under the source condition).

Suppose Assumption 3 hold. Then with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of 𝐒\mathbf{S}

M1−b≲𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≲M1−b.\displaystyle M^{1-b}\lesssim{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx}\lesssim M^{1-b}.

Here, the hidden constants only depend on the power-law degrees a,b.a,b.

Proof of Lemma C.5.

For the upper bound, by Lemma C.1 and noting 𝔼​𝐰i∗2≂ia−b{\mathbb{E}}\mathbf{w}^{*2}_{i}\eqsim i^{a-b} for all ii, we have with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}

𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle\mathsf{Approx} ≲∑k>k1λi​ia−b+(∑i>k1λiM+λk1+1+∑i>k1λi2M)⋅k11+a−b\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{k>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}i^{a-b}+\bigg(\frac{\sum_{i>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}}{M}+\lambda_{k_{1}+1}+\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}^{2}}{M}}\bigg)\cdot k_{1}^{1+a-b}
≲k11−b+(k11−aM+k1−a+k11−2​aM)​k11+a−b\displaystyle\lesssim k_{1}^{1-b}+\bigg(\frac{k_{1}^{1-a}}{M}+k_{1}^{-a}+\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}^{1-2a}}{M}}\bigg)k_{1}^{1+a-b}
≲(k1M+1)​k11−b\displaystyle\lesssim\bigg(\frac{k_{1}}{M}+1\bigg)k_{1}^{1-b}

for any given k1≤M/2k_{1}\leq M/2. Here the hidden constants depend on a,ba,b. Moreover, choosing k1=M/2k_{1}=M/2 in the upper bound gives

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx} ≲M1−b\displaystyle\lesssim M^{1-b}

with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}.

For the lower bound, we have from Lemma C.3 that

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≳∑i=M∞i−a⋅ia−b≳M1−b.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Approx}\gtrsim\sum_{i=M}^{\infty}i^{-a}\cdot i^{a-b}\gtrsim M^{1-b}.

This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma C.6 (Bounds on 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\mathsf{Approx} under the logarithmic power-law spectrum).

Suppose Assumption 4 hold. Then with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of 𝐒\mathbf{S}

log1−a⁡M≲𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≲log1−a⁡M.\displaystyle\log^{1-a}M\lesssim{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx}\lesssim\log^{1-a}M.

Here, the hidden constants only depend on the power-law degree a.a.

Proof of Lemma C.6.

For the upper bound, by Lemma C.1 and noting 𝔼​𝐰i∗2=1{\mathbb{E}}\mathbf{w}^{*2}_{i}=1 for all ii, we have with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}

𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle\mathsf{Approx} ≲∑k>k1λi+(∑i>k1λiM+λk1+1+∑i>k1λi2M)​k1\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{k>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}+\bigg(\frac{\sum_{i>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}}{M}+\lambda_{k_{1}+1}+\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}^{2}}{M}}\bigg)k_{1}
≲log1−a⁡k1+(log1−a⁡k1M+k1−1​log−a​k1+k11−2​aM)​k1\displaystyle\lesssim\log^{1-a}k_{1}+\bigg(\frac{\log^{1-a}k_{1}}{M}+k_{1}^{-1}\log^{-a}k_{1}+\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}^{1-2a}}{M}}\bigg)k_{1}
≲(1+k1M+1log⁡k1+1log⁡k1​k1M)​log1−a​k1\displaystyle\lesssim\bigg(1+\frac{k_{1}}{M}+\frac{1}{\log k_{1}}+\frac{1}{\log k_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{M}}\bigg)\log^{1-a}k_{1}
≲log1−a⁡k1\displaystyle\lesssim\log^{1-a}k_{1}

for any given k1≤M/2k_{1}\leq M/2, where the third line uses ∑i>k1λi2≲1/(k1​log2​a​k1)\sum_{i>k_{1}}\lambda_{i}^{2}\lesssim 1/(k_{1}\log^{2a}k_{1}). Choosing k1=M/2k_{1}=M/2, we obtain

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Approx} ≲log1−a⁡M\displaystyle\lesssim\log^{1-a}M

with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}. Here the hidden constants depend on a,ba,b.

For the lower bound, we have from Lemma C.2 that

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑≳∑i=M∞λi≳∑i=M∞i−1​log−a​i≳log1−a⁡M.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Approx}\gtrsim\sum_{i=M}^{\infty}\lambda_{i}\gtrsim\sum_{i=M}^{\infty}i^{-1}\log^{-a}i\gtrsim\log^{1-a}M.

Therefore, we have established matching upper and lower bounds for 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑.\mathsf{Approx}. ∎

Appendix D Bias error

In this section, we derive upper and lower bounds for 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗)\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) defined in Eq. (5). Moreover, we show that the upper and lower bounds match up to constant factors in concrete examples.

D.1 An upper bound

Lemma D.1 (Upper bound on the bias term).

Suppose the initial stepsize γ≤1c​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)\gamma\leq\frac{1}{c\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})} for some constant c>1c>1. Then for any 𝐰∗∈ℍ\mathbf{w}^{*}\in\mathbb{H} and k∈[d]k\in[d] such that r⁡(𝐇)≥k+Mr(\mathbf{H})\geq k+M, the bias term in (5) satisfies

𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗)≲1N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ​‖𝐯∗‖22.\displaystyle\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\lesssim\frac{1}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}\|{\mathbf{v}^{*}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Moreover, for any k≤M/3k\leq M/3 such that r⁡(𝐇)≥k+Mr(\mathbf{H})\geq k+M, the bias term satisfies

𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌(𝐰∗)≲∥𝐰∗0:k∥22N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ⋅[μM/2​(𝐀k)μM​(𝐀k)]2+∥𝐰k:∞∗∥𝐇k:∞2\displaystyle\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\lesssim\frac{\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k}}}\|_{2}^{2}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}\cdot\Bigg[\frac{\mu_{M/2}(\mathbf{A}_{k})}{\mu_{M}(\mathbf{A}_{k})}\Bigg]^{2}+\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k:\infty}}}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}_{{k:\infty}}}

with probability 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}, where 𝐀k:=𝐒k:∞𝐇k:∞𝐒k:∞⊤\mathbf{A}_{k}:=\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{H}_{{k:\infty}}\mathbf{S}_{{k:\infty}}^{\top}, {μi​(𝐀k)}i=1M\{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A}_{k})\}_{i=1}^{M} denote the eigenvalues of 𝐀k\mathbf{A}_{k} in non-increasing order for some constant c>1.c>1.

Proof of Lemma D.1.

Similar to the proof of Lemma C.1, we can without loss of generality assume the covariance matrix 𝐇=diag⁡{λ1,λ2,…,λd}\mathbf{H}=\diag\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{d}\} where λi≥λj\lambda_{i}\geq\lambda_{j} for any i≥ji\geq j. D.2 A lower bound

Lemma D.2 (Lower bound on the bias term).

Suppose 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} follows some prior distribution and the initial stepsize γ≤1c​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)\gamma\leq\frac{1}{c\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})} for some constant c>2c>2. Let 𝐇𝐰:=𝔼​𝐰∗​𝐰∗⁣⊤\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}:={\mathbb{E}}\mathbf{w}^{*}\mathbf{w}^{*\top}. Then the bias term in Eq. (5) satisfies

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) ≳∑i:λ~i<1/(γ​N𝚎𝚏𝚏)μi​(𝐒𝐇𝐇𝐰​𝐇𝐒⊤)μi​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)\displaystyle\gtrsim\sum_{i:\tilde{\lambda}_{i}<1/(\gamma N_{\mathtt{eff}})}\frac{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})}{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})}

almost surely.

Proof of Lemma D.2.

where the third line uses 𝐈M−2​γt​𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤≻𝟎M\mathbf{I}_{M}-2\gamma_{t}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\succ{\mathbf{0}}_{M} for all t∈[N]t\in[N] established in the proof of Lemma D.1, ∑i=1N/N𝚎𝚏𝚏γN𝚎𝚏𝚏​i≤2​γ\sum_{i=1}^{N/N_{\mathtt{eff}}}\gamma_{N_{\mathtt{eff}}i}\leq 2\gamma, and the fact that (1−w)​(1−v)≥1−w−v(1-w)(1-v)\geq 1-w-v for w,v>0w,v>0. D.3 Examples on matching bounds for 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗)\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})

In this section, we derive matching upper and lower bounds for 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌⁡(𝐰∗)\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) in (5) in three scenarios: power-law spectrum (Lemma D.3), power-law spectrum with source condition (Lemma D.4) and logarithmic power-law spectrum (Lemma D.5). Recall that we define 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌:=𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)\mathsf{Bias}:={\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

Lemma D.3 (Bounds on 𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌\mathsf{Bias} under the power-law spectrum).

Suppose Assumption 1C and 2 hold and the initial stepsize γ≤1c​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)\gamma\leq\frac{1}{c\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})} for some constant c>2c>2. Then with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of 𝐒\mathbf{S}

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)≲max⁡{(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a−1,M1−a},\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\lesssim\max\big\{(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}-1},\ M^{1-{a}}\big\},

and

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)≳(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a−1\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\gtrsim(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}-1}

when (N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a≤M/c(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}}\leq M/c for some constant c>0c>0. Here, all the (hidden) constants depend only on the power-law degree a.a.

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) ≲𝔼𝐰∗[∥𝐰∗0:k2∥22N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ+∥𝐰k2:∞∗∥𝐇k2:∞2]\displaystyle\lesssim{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\Bigg[\frac{\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k_{2}}}}\|_{2}^{2}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}+\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k_{2}:\infty}}}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}_{{k_{2}:\infty}}}\Bigg]
≲k2N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ+∑k>k2λi\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{k_{2}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}+\sum_{k>k_{2}}\lambda_{i}
≂k2N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ+k21−a\displaystyle\eqsim\frac{k_{2}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}+k_{2}^{1-a}
≲max⁡{(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a−1,M1−a},\displaystyle\lesssim\max\big\{(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}-1},\ M^{1-{a}}\big\},

where in the last inequality, we choose k2=[M/3]∧(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/ak_{2}=[M/3]\wedge(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}} to minimize the upper bound.

When (N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a≤M/3(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}}\leq M/3, combining Lemma D.2 and G.4 gives the lower bound

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathbf{w}^{*}}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) ≳∑i:λ~i<1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)μi​(𝐒𝐇𝐇𝐰​𝐇𝐒⊤)μi​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)=∑i:λ~i<1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)μi​(𝐒𝐇2​𝐒⊤)μi​(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤),\displaystyle\gtrsim\sum_{i:\tilde{\lambda}_{i}<1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)}\frac{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}^{\mathbf{w}}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})}{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})}=\sum_{i:\tilde{\lambda}_{i}<1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)}\frac{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}^{2}\mathbf{S}^{\top})}{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})},
≳∑λ~i<1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ),i≤Mi−2​ai−a=∑λi<1/(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ),i≤Mi−a≳(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a−1\displaystyle\gtrsim\sum_{\tilde{\lambda}_{i}<1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma),i\leq M}\frac{i^{-2a}}{i^{-a}}=\sum_{\lambda_{i}<1/(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma),i\leq M}i^{-a}\gtrsim(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}-1}

with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}. Here, the hidden constants depend only on a.a. ∎

Suppose Assumption 3 hold and the initial stepsize γ≤1c​tr⁡(𝐒𝐇𝐒⊤)\gamma\leq\frac{1}{c\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}^{\top})} for some constant c>2c>2. Then with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of 𝐒\mathbf{S}

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)≲max⁡{(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)(1−b)/a,M1−b},\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\lesssim\max\big\{(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{(1-b)/a},\ M^{1-b}\big\},

and

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)≳(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)(1−b)/a\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\gtrsim(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{(1-b)/a}

when (N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)1/a≤M/c(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{1/{a}}\leq M/c for some constant c>0c>0. Moreover, when b≥a+1b\geq a+1, with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)} over the randomness of 𝐒\mathbf{S}

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)≲log⁡N𝚎𝚏𝚏⋅max⁡{(N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ)(1−b)/a,M1−b}\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\lesssim\log N_{\mathtt{eff}}\cdot\max\big\{(N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma)^{(1-b)/a},\ M^{1-b}\big\}

In all results, the hidden constants depend only on a,b.a,b.

Proof of Lemma D.4.

For the upper bound, using Lemma G.5, D.1 and the assumption that (w.l.o.g.) 𝔼​𝐰i∗2≂ia−b{\mathbb{E}}{\mathbf{w}^{*2}_{i}}\eqsim i^{a-b} for all i>0i>0, with probability at least 1−e−Ω⁡(M)1-e^{-\Omega(M)}, we have

𝔼𝐰∗​𝖡𝗂𝖺𝗌​(𝐰∗)\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\mathsf{Bias}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) ≲𝔼𝐰∗[∥𝐰∗0:k2∥22N𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ+∥𝐰k2:∞∗∥𝐇k2:∞2]\displaystyle\lesssim{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}\Bigg[\frac{\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{0:k_{2}}}}\|_{2}^{2}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}+\|{\mathbf{w}^{*}_{{k_{2}:\infty}}}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{H}_{{k_{2}:\infty}}}\Bigg]
≲k21+a−bN𝚎𝚏𝚏​γ+∑k>k2λi⋅ia−b\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{k_{2}^{1+a-b}}{N_{\mathtt{eff}}\gamma}+\sum_{k>k_{2}}\lambda_{i}\cdot i^{a-b}
